intro:
These exercises practice the one habit the chapter keeps returning to: a gRPC service is two things at once — a protobuf contract shared across languages and a pile of generated Rust code — and the engineer's job is to keep them in their place. You will choose the right RPC shape from the data flow rather than from novelty, keep generated transport types from leaking into the domain model, build the small adapter seam that converts one generated request into one application command, and reason about deadlines, cancellation, backpressure, and status codes as parts of the API rather than as runtime accidents.

The lab and the implementation exercise both center on the same mapping seam, because that seam is where most real bugs hide and where unit testing pays off even when the live service runs on tonic. The debugging, evolution, and design exercises then widen the lens to the polyglot fleet: what counts as a breaking change to a contract that Go, C#, and C++ also generate from, what gates belong in CI, and what a production service lane needs before rollout. Throughout, the wire is rarely the surprise. The surprise is what each ecosystem used to do for you automatically that Rust now asks you to state explicitly.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose unary, server streaming, client streaming, or bidirectional streaming from the contract
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Classify each endpoint by asking who sends once, who sends many times, and who controls the pace. The position of the stream keyword in the rpc line is the whole difference between the four shapes, so the question is which side fans out and which side fans in.

Create one invoice is a unary call: one request in, one response out. The client sends a single CreateInvoiceRequest, the server validates and persists it, and a single CreateInvoiceResponse (or a status) comes back. There is no accumulation and no open-ended pacing, so anything fancier than unary would add a lifecycle and buffer contract the workload does not need.

Watch invoice events over time wants server streaming: one request opens one subscription, and the server then fans out a sequence of event messages until the subscription ends or the client disconnects. The pacing implication is immediate — the server is now the producer and the client is the consumer, so you need a bounded buffer between event production and the network, and you must treat a client disconnect as a stop signal rather than keep producing into a dead channel.

Upload many invoices then get one summary wants client streaming: the client owns accumulation, sending many invoice messages, and the server replies with exactly one summary after the client signals end-of-stream. The buffering question here lives on the server's fan-in side — how much in-flight data it will hold while folding the stream into a running summary, and whether it bounds that to avoid a slow or hostile client pinning memory.

The long-lived sync conversation, where both peers keep sending updates with no fixed one-to-one ordering, is the only endpoint that truly wants bidirectional streaming. The backpressure question that appears immediately is: when one side produces faster than the other consumes, where does the slack go? You must decide on a bounded send queue per direction and a policy for what happens when it fills — block the producer, shed messages, or close the stream — because a bidirectional stream with no boundedness policy is still unfinished. The trap the exercise warns against is reaching for bidirectional streaming by default; three of the four endpoints are served by simpler, cheaper shapes.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The same four endpoints expressed as protobuf rpc lines; the stream keyword's position is the classification.
criteria: Each workload is mapped to a shape with a transport reason: unary for create, server streaming for the subscription, client streaming for the upload-and-summarize, bidirectional for the sync conversation.

Pacing implications are named for the streaming cases: bounded buffer plus disconnect-as-stop for server streaming, bounded fan-in for client streaming, per-direction send-queue policy for bidirectional.
Bidirectional is reserved for the one endpoint whose data flow genuinely requires it; the other three use simpler shapes.

exerciseSolutions.title: Read generated transport types without contaminating the domain model
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect to spot is that the service method accepts a generated CreateInvoiceRequest and passes it unchanged into a domain aggregate constructor. A generated protobuf message is a transport type: it carries field tags, serialization rules, optional/default semantics from the wire format, and whatever shape the .proto happened to commit to for cross-language compatibility. Those are transport concerns, not domain concerns. The moment the aggregate constructor takes that type, the domain depends on the wire schema, and every additive protobuf change starts to look like domain churn.

Look at the request in Example 1 (grpc_transport_to_domain_mapping). The customer_id: String and line_totals: Vec<u64> are owned input that the transport already deserialized for you. Whether a string can be empty, whether a vector can be zero-length, the field numbering — those are properties of the deserialized message, not invariants the domain wants. The domain wants a non-empty customer and a non-empty invoice; the request type cannot guarantee either.

Tenant, caller identity, and other metadata-derived fields are the clearest tell. They do not live in the request body at all — they arrive in per-call gRPC metadata (the protobuf equivalent of HTTP headers) and are pulled out by an interceptor before the handler runs. They must be attached outside the generated message, at the adapter seam, precisely because the generated message has no field for them and should not grow one. In the chapter's code that is exactly the tenant parameter handed to into_command separately from the request.

The hand-written command type that makes the boundary calmer is CreateInvoiceCommand: tenant plus the validated, owned customer and line totals. It is the application service's contract, not the transport's. Once that mapping seam exists explicitly, three things get easier to test and refactor. Validation becomes a pure function you can unit test with no gRPC runtime, no tonic, and no metadata mocking. The domain stops recompiling when the .proto changes additively, because only the adapter touches the generated type. And the service signature reads in domain language, so a missing customer or empty invoice is rejected at the edge and never reaches InvoiceService::create.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The seam: generated request on the transport side, hand-written command on the domain side, tenant attached from metadata.
criteria: Generated DTOs (CreateInvoiceRequest, with field tags and wire defaults) are distinguished from the application command (CreateInvoiceCommand).
Tenant (and caller identity) are identified as metadata-derived fields attached at the adapter, outside the generated message code.
At least one benefit of the seam is named: pure-function testability of validation, and domain insulation from additive .proto changes.

exerciseSolutions.title: Map a generated request into a domain command
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Implement into_command as the entire transport boundary: it validates the generated request, moves its owned fields into a separate CreateInvoiceCommand, and returns a typed result. The validation is two explicit checks that mirror the domain's invariants — reject an empty customer id and reject an empty line set — and only on success does the function construct the command. This is the same seam you would unit test heavily even if the live service ran on tonic, which is why it is worth getting exactly right.

The ownership move is the point. CreateInvoiceRequest already owns its String and its Vec<u64>; the generated message deserialized them once. So the adapter moves them — request.customer_id and request.line_totals are moved field-by-field into the command, not cloned. Cloning here would allocate a second copy of data the transport is about to drop anyway. Data is owned once at the transport edge and moved into the application command exactly once, which is both cheaper and the idiomatic expression of "this value now belongs to the domain."

Keep the error type small and transport-facing. In the lab the result error is &'static str, which is fine for the runnable program; in the chapter's fuller Example 1 it is a TransportError enum (MissingCustomer, EmptyInvoice) so the adapter can map each shape problem to a distinct gRPC status later. Either way the error is the adapter's vocabulary, not the domain's — the downstream service never sees a Status, a Request wrapper, or a metadata API.

The returned command is deliberately a different type from the request. That is what lets the rest of the system depend on CreateInvoiceCommand without depending on gRPC. The lab then prints tenant, customer, and the summed total cents from the mapped command, proving the data crossed the seam intact.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The adapter: validate two transport-shape problems, then move owned fields into a separate command type.
criteria: The mapping returns CreateInvoiceCommand, a distinct type from the generated CreateInvoiceRequest.
The adapter validates at least two transport-shape problems explicitly: empty customer id and empty line set.
The runnable lab prints tenant = acme, customer = cust-7, total cents = 4200 from the mapped command.
The error type and signature keep gRPC out of the downstream service: no Request wrapper, Status, or metadata API leaks past the seam.

exerciseSolutions.title: Diagnose a deadline, cancellation, or streaming backpressure bug
exerciseSolutions.solution:
There are two distinct defects, and both are the same underlying mistake: work keeps flowing after the caller or the stream has already said stop. Treat them separately because the repairs differ.

The unary handler keeps doing CPU-heavy work after the deadline has expired. The fix is to check the deadline at meaningful work boundaries, not once at entry. Read the remaining time before each expensive stage (and inside any loop over a large input), and as soon as elapsed exceeds the deadline, stop and return Status DeadlineExceeded rather than burning a core computing a result no one will read. In the chapter's Example 2 (grpc_status_deadline_retry) this is exactly what should_abort(deadline_ms, elapsed_ms, cancelled) expresses: abort when cancelled or when elapsed has reached the deadline. The principle is that a deadline is part of the API contract — the caller told you how long the answer is worth — so honoring it is correctness, not optimization.

The streaming handler keeps buffering items into a local channel after the client disconnects. This has two bugs layered on top of each other. The first is an ownership bug that exists even before cancellation: the buffer is unbounded, so a slow or absent consumer lets producers pin unbounded memory. Bound it — use a fixed-capacity channel — so that when the consumer falls behind, the producer feels backpressure (the send blocks or yields Err) instead of growing the queue forever. A disconnected client is a pacing signal, not a transport curiosity. The second bug is the missing cancellation check: when the send side reports the receiver is gone, or the stream's cancellation token fires, the producer must stop and drop its work, because continuing to produce into a dead stream is wasted CPU and a slow-leak of in-flight resources.

For status codes: surface DeadlineExceeded when the server gives up because the deadline passed, and Cancelled when the caller actively cancelled or disconnected. Importantly, Cancelled is not retryable — the caller chose to stop — whereas DeadlineExceeded on an idempotent call may be. To prove the repair helped, instrument the observable signals the API now exposes: the count of in-flight stream items (it should stop growing without bound), a cancelled-RPC counter, and a deadline-exceeded counter. A trace field recording deadline_remaining_ms at the point of abort, plus queue age or queue depth on the streaming buffer, lets you confirm that work actually stops near the limit rather than well past it.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Deadline and cancellation checks at work boundaries, plus a bounded channel that turns a stalled consumer into backpressure.
criteria: A deadline/cancellation check is placed at a real work boundary (per stage / per loop iteration), not only at handler entry.
The streaming buffer is bounded (sync_channel with fixed capacity) so a stalled or disconnected consumer produces backpressure instead of unbounded growth.
DeadlineExceeded vs Cancelled status codes are chosen correctly, and observability signals (in-flight items, cancelled-RPC count, deadline-exceeded count, queue age) are named to prove the repair.

exerciseSolutions.title: Test generated APIs and prevent breaking protobuf changes
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Classify the three changes first, because the CI gates follow from the classification. Adding one field with a new field number is additive and safe: old peers that do not know the field ignore it, and the wire identity of every existing field is untouched. Removing a field is breaking unless handled correctly — the danger is not that old code stops compiling, it is that the freed field number could later be reused for a different type and silently misread old data on the wire. Changing a method from unary to streaming is the largest break of the three: it changes the RPC shape, so every generated client and server signature for that method changes, and stale-generated peers will fail to talk to the new service. The rule of thumb is that protobuf evolution must be additive and boring; method-shape changes are neither.

The contract artifact to diff in CI is the .proto schema itself (or a descriptor set / FileDescriptorSet derived from it), checked in and compared against the previous version. A breaking-change linter such as buf is the standard tool: it flags field-number reuse, removed-without-reserved fields, type changes, and method-shape changes as build failures. This is the gate that matters most because it runs before a partner team regenerates from a stale or incompatible contract — schema drift becomes a build failure, not a post-rollout surprise. Treating broken codegen drift as merely "the Rust server still compiles locally" misses the point: it is still contract drift for everyone else.

Two kinds of transport test should run against generated code. First, a compile/contract test that simply regenerates client and server from the current .proto and builds them in CI — that catches the unary-to-streaming break immediately, because the trait and client signatures no longer match. Second, a round-trip test that constructs a generated message, serializes and deserializes it, and asserts the values survive, plus a small generated-client-to-generated-server test that exercises at least one method end to end. These are cheap and they fail loudly when the wire shape moves.

Finally, the policy must reserve removed field tags and names. After deleting a field, mark its number and its name reserved in the message (reserved 4; reserved "old_field";) so no future edit can recycle the tag for a new, incompatible type or recycle the name in a way that confuses readers. Reserving is the cheap insurance that turns a future foot-gun into a compile-time complaint.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Additive vs breaking changes, reserved tags/names, and the CI gates that catch drift before partners regenerate.
criteria: At least one additive change (new field with new number) and one breaking change (removed field, or unary-to-streaming method) are classified correctly.
A schema-drift / breaking-change CI gate is defined (descriptor diff or a buf breaking check that fails the build).
A generated-client/server compile test and a serialize/deserialize round-trip test are named.
Removed field tags and names are explicitly reserved in the policy.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design a polyglot gRPC service lane with auth, tracing, and retries
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Design the billing service as a contract first and a Rust implementation second, because Go workers, a C# admin tool, and a C++ plugin all generate from the same .proto and consume the same operational guidance. Three artifacts are public: the .proto, the retry policy, and the metadata contract. Everything below is stated so another language team can adopt it without reading Rust.

Metadata on every call and stream session. Require an authorization token (a bearer credential in the authorization metadata key) and reject its absence with Unauthenticated before any handler runs — that rejection belongs in a server interceptor, the seam that reads metadata and either fails fast or inserts a typed caller context. Also require a tenant id and trace-propagation headers. For tracing, propagate W3C traceparent (and tracestate) on every call so a request that fans out across the Go worker, the Rust service, and the C++ plugin stitches into one trace; the interceptor reads the incoming traceparent, starts a server span as its child, and injects the propagated context onto any downstream call the handler makes. The caller-context rule and the trace-propagation rule together make the boundary observable and authorized before business logic begins.

Retry and idempotency classification. Use the chapter's classify(status, idempotent) discipline (Example 2, grpc_status_deadline_retry): Unavailable and DeadlineExceeded are retryable but only for idempotent methods, with exponential backoff and jitter; Cancelled is terminal because the caller chose to stop; InvalidArgument, FailedPrecondition, and the other caller-fault codes are terminal — retrying them just repeats the same rejection. The idempotency rule is the gate: CreateInvoice must carry a client-supplied idempotency key so a retried Unavailable cannot double-bill, and read-only methods are idempotent by construction and freely retryable. Publish this table alongside the .proto so every language's retry interceptor agrees.

Stream boundedness and concurrency. The streaming routes — WatchInvoiceEvents (server streaming) and any Sync (bidirectional) method — get explicit, per-route budgets: a bounded send queue per stream (so a slow consumer produces backpressure instead of unbounded memory growth), a cap on concurrent open streams per caller, and a maximum stream lifetime after which the server closes with a resumable cursor. A stream without a boundedness policy is under-specified for production, so this is a contract clause, not an implementation detail.

Telemetry before rollout. Ship at least: status-code-family counters (OK / caller-fault / server-fault, so you can see whether errors are 'their fault' or 'ours'); cancelled-RPC and deadline-exceeded counters; stream lifetime and in-flight-stream-item gauges per streaming route; and queue age / depth on the bounded send queues so a backpressure problem shows up as rising age before it shows up as an outage. With those four hooks, retries, cancellation, and stream pacing are observable from day one rather than diagnosed after the first incident.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Shared retry classification plus the interceptor and streaming-budget rules the polyglot contract must publish.
criteria: An auth/caller-context rule (authorization token -> Unauthenticated, typed CallerContext) and a trace-propagation rule (W3C traceparent, child span) are both defined.
Retryable (Unavailable, DeadlineExceeded under idempotency + key) vs terminal (Cancelled, InvalidArgument, FailedPrecondition) behavior is classified explicitly.
At least one boundedness/concurrency rule is included for a streaming path (bounded send queue, concurrent-stream cap, max lifetime).
At least three observability hooks are named: status-code-family counters, cancelled/deadline counters, stream lifetime, and queue age.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
tenant = acme
customer = cust-7
total cents = 4200
labSolution.explanation:
into_command is the entire transport boundary. It first runs two validation checks: a trimmed-empty customer id and an empty line set are both rejected before any command exists, so a malformed request never reaches the application layer. Only on success does it construct a CreateInvoiceCommand. The tenant arrives as a separate &str argument — standing in for a value an interceptor would pull from per-call metadata — and is owned by the command via tenant.to_string(), while the request's customer_id String and line_totals Vec are moved field-by-field rather than cloned, because the request owns them already and is about to be dropped.

main builds a request for cust-7 with line totals of 1200 and 3000 cents, maps it under tenant acme, and unwraps the Ok. It then sums the line totals with iter().copied().sum::<u64>(), giving 1200 + 3000 = 4200. The three println! lines read straight off the mapped command and its derived total, producing tenant = acme, customer = cust-7, and total cents = 4200.

The whole program compiles with only the standard library: it is the mapping seam in isolation, with no tonic, no protobuf runtime, and no async — which is exactly the point of the exercise, since this seam is unit-testable as a pure function regardless of what transport the live service uses.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should generated protobuf types usually stop at the transport boundary instead of becoming the domain model?
reviewAnswers.answer: Generated protobuf messages are transport types: they carry field tags, wire defaults, and a cross-language shape chosen for compatibility, none of which are domain invariants. If the domain depends on them directly, every additive .proto change looks like domain churn and the business logic recompiles for reasons that have nothing to do with the business. Keeping them at the boundary and mapping into a hand-written command lets validation become a pure, testable function and insulates the domain from schema evolution.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes field tags more durable than field names in protobuf evolution?
reviewAnswers.answer: Field tags (the = 1, = 2 numbers) are what actually go on the wire; names are a source-level convenience that the encoder discards. You can rename a field freely and old serialized data still decodes, because decoding matches by number, but reusing or changing a number silently misreads existing data and breaks every peer that generated against the old schema. That is why the durable identity is the number, and why removed numbers must be reserved so they are never recycled.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are deadlines, cancellation, and backpressure part of the API design rather than only runtime behavior?
reviewAnswers.answer: A deadline is the caller stating how long the answer is worth, cancellation is the caller withdrawing the request, and backpressure is the contract for what happens when a producer outpaces a consumer — all three are promises the two sides must agree on, not incidental runtime details. A streaming method with vague message rate, buffer size, and cancellation rules is an unfinished design, because an unbounded buffer is an ownership bug and ignored cancellation wastes work the caller no longer wants. Designing them in means choosing bounded queues, deadline checks at work boundaries, and explicit stop signals as part of the method's specification.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between a retryable Unavailable and a non-retryable InvalidArgument?
reviewAnswers.answer: Unavailable means 'I am temporarily unable; the same request might succeed later', so an idempotent call should retry it with backoff. InvalidArgument means 'your request is malformed; fix it and stop retrying', so retrying just repeats the same rejection and wastes capacity. The status code is chosen by what the caller should do next, not by the internal cause, which is what makes a shared retry policy possible across every language that generates from the contract.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should generated client and server artifacts be rebuilt or checked in CI whenever the .proto changes?
reviewAnswers.answer: The .proto is a shared contract that Go, C#, C++, and Rust all regenerate from, so a change that compiles fine in the Rust server can still break partners who regenerate stale or incompatible code. Rebuilding generated client and server in CI, plus a breaking-change check (buf breaking) and a serialize/deserialize round-trip test, catches method-shape changes and field-number reuse before any partner regenerates. That turns schema drift into a build failure rather than a post-rollout incident, which is the cheapest place to catch it.
